short: Relay stations a day's ride apart let Mongol couriers cross Eurasia at 300 kilometres a day.
full:
The yam, or örtöö, was a chain of relay posts set roughly 30 to 50 kilometres apart along the empire's main routes. Each held remounts, fodder, provisions and shelter, maintained by the surrounding population as a tax obligation. Ögedei Khan extended it across the whole empire around 1234. A courier carrying a paiza — an inscribed tablet of wood, bronze, silver or gold according to rank — could demand a fresh horse at every station and ride on, covering in a week distances that took a caravan two months.

It was built for military intelligence, and it worked: Karakorum could hear from Persia or northern China in a fortnight. Its side effects were larger. Merchants, envoys and clerics moved along the same roads under the same protection, which is how the Polos reached Kublai's court and how papal friars reached Karakorum. The system survived the empire's division, each khanate running its own section, and decayed in China with the Yuan collapse of 1368, though relay posts on the steppe outlasted it by centuries.
